daily.title: Section 271(1)(c) Penalty Cannot Survive Once Section 14A Disallowance Is Set Aside
daily.summary: ITAT Delhi deletes Rs.51.15 lakh penalty under Section 271(1)(c) after the underlying Section 14A disallowance was remanded for fresh computation. The Delhi ITAT held that a penalty under section 271(1)(c) cannot survive once the disallowance on which it was levied has been set aside and restored to the Assessing Officer for fresh computation . Although the CIT(A) recognised that the original disallowance no longer sustained the penalty, it dismissed the penalty appeal as infructuous. The Tribunal granted substantive relief by deleting the penalty of ₹51,14,629 and allowing the assessee’s appeal.

daily.title: Section 56(2)(x): Agreement-Date Stamp Duty Value Applies Where Advance Paid Earlier
daily.summary: ITAT Lucknow directs recomputation of Rs.66.47 lakh addition under Section 56(2)(x) using agreement-date stamp duty value as advance was paid earlier. The Lucknow ITAT held that where a prior agreement fixes the purchase consideration and part of that consideration has been paid by cheque before the agreement, the stamp duty value on the agreement date applies for computing the buyer’s income under section 56(2)(x) . The Tribunal directed the Assessing Officer to ascertain the value on 16 August 2010 , the date of the agreement produced on record, and recompute the addition.

daily.title: Senior Citizen Tax Rates For Tax Year 2026-27: With Example on Different Income Levels

Tax Year 2026–27 is the same period as FY 2026–27 (AY 2027–28) under the older terminology. Tax is progressive, so each rate applies only to the income inside its band. A 4% Health and Education Cess is added on top, and a surcharge applies at higher incomes.

daily.title: Demonetisation Cash Deposits: Cash-Flow Evidence Cannot Be Rejected Without Reasons
daily.summary: The Rajkot ITAT held that an Assessing Officer cannot disregard cash books, bank statements and cash-flow statements supporting the source of demonetisation deposits without explaining why the evidence is unreliable. In this case, the Tribunal found that the cash-flow statement showed sufficient cash on hand and that the Assessing Officer had failed to address the supporting records. The Tribunal nevertheless considered some of the material self-serving and restricted the addition from ₹16,90,000 to ₹1,00,000 . It directed that the amount sustained be taxed at normal income-tax rates, without applying section 115BBE .
